extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, scientists, and readers interested in the method of scientific inquiry and the communication of results
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how to conduct experimental inquiry, derive causes from effects, choose and design decisive experiments, and when/how to communicate or publish results so as to advance collective scientific knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to promote general good by communicating discoveries
rubrics_metrics.description: Belief that one is bound to promote, as far as in us lies, the general good of mankind by communicating discoveries which can be useful in life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communicate findings to incite others to contribute experiments and discoveries, so that by beginning where predecessors left off and connecting many labours, collective progress exceeds isolated efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish tested results and treat writing as if for public scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Commit to writing all results 'as soon as I should have tested their truth, and to bestow the same care upon them as I would have done had it been my design to publish them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preparing work with the care for publication improves scrutiny and correctness; what is thought true may appear false when forced into written form, so test thoroughly before communicating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer experiments increasingly as knowledge advances
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiments become always more necessary the more one is advanced in knowledge; at the commencement it is better to use what is presented to the senses, but later experiment is required to resolve finer questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early stages: rely on common sense observations. Later stages: design and perform many particular experiments to resolve subtle distinctions and detect causes of particular effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin from simple, common phenomena before tackling rare ones
rubrics_metrics.description: At the commencement, it is better to make use only of what is spontaneously presented to our senses ... than to concern ourselves about more uncommon and recondite phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study the most ordinary effects first because uncommon phenomena often mislead until the causes of ordinary ones are known; build knowledge stepwise from the simple to the complex.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of inquiry: deduce causes from self-evident truths, then ordinary effects, then particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: First find principles or first causes from certain germs of truths naturally existing in our minds; second, examine the first and most ordinary effects deducible from these causes; then descend to particulars by experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a top-down logical order but confirm by experiment: derive a chain from first principles to effects and use experiments to bridge from general causes to specific particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design decisive experiments to distinguish competing explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple modes could explain an effect, seek experiments 'such that their result is not the same, if it is in the one of these modes ... as it would be if it were to be explained in the other.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolve explanatory ambiguity by devising experiments whose outcomes differ depending on which explanation is true, enabling selection between competing theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Label provisional claims as hypotheses to prevent misuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Call some propositions hypotheses and be indifferent about giving proof of them when appropriate, so that others will not build extravagant philosophies upon them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly mark statements that are not yet fully demonstrated to avoid misinterpretation and irresponsible extension by less cautious minds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select materials for communication that avoid unnecessary controversy
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose matters to publish that 'should neither be obnoxious to much controversy, nor should compel me to expound more of my principles than I desired, and which should yet be sufficient clearly to exhibit what I can or cannot accomplish in the sciences.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When presenting specimens of work, prefer examples that demonstrate method and capability without provoking distracting disputes or requiring full disclosure of all underlying principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about publishing if it will divert time from research
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolve not to consent to publication during life, lest oppositions or controversies or gained reputation 'should be any occasion of my losing the time that I had set apart for my own improvement.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh the costs of public controversy and reputational distraction against the benefit of communicating results; avoid premature publication that would impede further discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare to acknowledge errors publicly when convinced
rubrics_metrics.description: Engage to 'with perfect frankness to avow my errors if I am convinced of them,' and otherwise succinctly state what is required to defend the matters written.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage open correction: invite objections via publisher and reply concisely; accept demonstrated errors rather than defending mistaken positions at all costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor demonstrable truth over rhetorical victory
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticizes scholastic disputations where each strives for victory and 'is much more occupied in making the best of mere verisimilitude, than in weighing the reasons on both sides of the question.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid argumentative tactics aimed at winning; emphasize careful weighing of reasons and empirical support rather than rhetorical skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of others' poorly described or biased experiments; prefer replication
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiments made by others are often 'accompanied with so many circumstances and superfluous elements' and 'so ill described, or even so false ... that ... their value could not compensate for the time necessary to make the selection.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat reported experiments skeptically: re-run or redesign experiments rather than relying on poorly described accounts; expect bias from experimenters who see only what conforms to their principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use skilled artisans with remuneration for precise experimental work
rubrics_metrics.description: One man is not equal to making all experiments; he can advantageously avail himself of artisans or parties of the same kind whom he could pay, whose hope of gain might stimulate accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When experimental skill is required, employ and compensate capable artisans to achieve the precision necessary; unsolicited volunteer help is often unreliable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote cumulative science by sharing methods and results
rubrics_metrics.description: Communicate little discoveries to incite men of superior genius to contribute experiments and inform the public of their discoveries, 'so that, by the last beginning where those before them had left off ... we might collectively proceed much farther.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publish methods and results in ways that let successors continue the work sequentially; emphasize reproducibility and sufficient detail to permit others to build on findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer publication in the vernacular to reach unprejudiced judges
rubrics_metrics.description: Writes in French rather than Latin 'because I expect that those who make use of their unprejudiced natural reason will be better judges of my opinions than those who give heed to the writings of the ancients only.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a language and presentation accessible to the intended critical audience rather than relying solely on traditional scholarly forms that may bias evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid trusting hearsay about authorship; rely on original publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Requests posterity 'never to believe on hearsay that anything has proceeded from me which has not been published by myself.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For attribution and scholarly credit, rely on primary publications; be cautious of secondhand reports that may misrepresent original thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for practical utility (medicine) as a chief scientific end
rubrics_metrics.description: The end of this inquiry is practical: 'to discover a practical [method] ... and thus render ourselves the lords and possessors of nature' particularly to improve medicine, 'for the preservation of health ... is ... the first and fundamental' blessing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Orient investigations toward applications that improve human well-being, especially medical knowledge and remedies; value practical outcomes alongside theoretical understanding.
